title: Neural network AI models address foundational topics in fisheries science, including forecasting and harvest optimization
content:
Abstract
The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents novel opportunities for tackling complex marine resource management challenges. Among AI models, neural networks (NNs) are a powerful class of tools capable of learning nonlocal and lagged patterns from fisheries data as well as approximating nonlinear relationships among multiple latent variables using estimation methods that automatically implement statistical shrinkage. This gives them potential to effectively handle data obtained from fisheries populations subject to dynamic environments. We highlight three applications of NNs: Long short-term memory (LSTM) and convolutional neural network (CNNs) and policy discovery via reinforcement learning. LSTMs are designed to handle sequential data by allowing prediction from past values at both short and long time-lags. CNNs are not explicitly designed to handle temporal information, but can interpolate a spatial latent variable based on its value within a geographic neighborhood, and can be combined with LSTM models for this purpose. This “Food for Thought” paper introduces and applies these NN approaches, both alone and in combination, to demonstrate their potential application for several foundational topics in fisheries science: (i) the forecasting of population weight-at-age, (ii) the standardization of spatio-temporal indices of relative abundance, and (iii) the discovery of harvest policies to optimize catches and maintain spawning biomass. Each section provides a simple, simulated example and describes the tradeoffs—particularly the lack of inferential capability—presented by using NNs over traditional approaches for each topic. We then outline medium-term research questions that may clarify, facilitate, or qualify the applicability of these tools to fisheries management science.
